analysis.one_liner: Forces companies to sell their pharmacies if they also own a drug-price middleman or health insurer.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 13, 2026 by one Democrat with two Republican and one Democratic cosponsors, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes it illegal for one company to own a pharmacy and also own a health insurer or a pharmacy benefit manager — the middlemen that decide which drugs plans cover, what patients pay, and how much pharmacies get reimbursed. Companies that currently have both, like the largest insurers that also own PBMs and pharmacy chains, would have one year to sell off their pharmacies. Federal agencies, state attorneys general, and private citizens could sue to enforce the breakup, and the FTC and Justice Department could block future deals that recreate the same conflicts.
analysis.who_benefits: People who fill prescriptions, whose drug prices are shaped by a handful of companies, and independent pharmacies that have been squeezed by contracts with the largest PBMs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug users and independent pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any company from owning a pharmacy while also owning an insurance company or a pharmacy benefit manager, with a one-year deadline to divest the pharmacy [S2]
Targets a conflict the FTC has already found: vertically integrated PBMs can steer prescriptions to their own affiliated pharmacies, which reduces competition and raises drug costs for patients [S2]
Gives the FTC and Justice Department antitrust division joint enforcement power, and lets state attorneys general and individual patients sue, with triple damages available and jury trial rights [S2]

Implements a real penalty for delay: companies that miss divestment milestones must transfer 10 percent of their profits into escrow every month, forfeited if they fail to divest in time, with a trustee empowered to sell the pharmacy for them [S2]

Requires any revenue a company earned through the illegal combination to be disgorged into a fund used for the health care needs of the harmed community, including consumers overcharged at affiliated pharmacies [S2]

analysis.who_pays: The largest health conglomerates — companies that own an insurer, a PBM, and a pharmacy business — would have to sell their pharmacy operations within a year, and their shareholders would bear the lost value and transition costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: CVS, UnitedHealth, Cigna and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The one-year divestment deadline covers every kind of pharmacy, including mail-order, specialty, hospital, and long-term care pharmacies, so unwinding these businesses quickly could disrupt access for patients who rely on affiliated specialty or mail-order services [S2]

The bill attacks only common ownership; it does not directly cap drug prices or regulate how PBMs set reimbursement rates, so savings for patients depend on whether breaking up the conglomerates actually restores competition [S2]

Forced divestment of pharmacy operations worth tens of billions of dollars would impose significant one-time transaction and restructuring costs and create uncertainty in the drug supply chain during the transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is well supported by the record: the FTC has found that integrated PBMs steer business to their own pharmacies and raise costs, and the bill gives agencies and patients real tools to enforce a breakup. The honest risks are the speed of a one-year divestment and the fact that ownership separation alone does not guarantee lower prices — it removes a documented conflict of interest but leaves PBM market concentration in place.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled with about seven months left in the two-year session.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 13, 2026 together with Sens. Josh Hawley, John Fetterman, and Roger Marshall [S2]
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and the action history shows no further steps [S4]

The bill's findings note that the six largest PBMs processed more than 90 percent of U.S. prescriptions in 2023 and are each integrated into large health conglomerates with retail, mail-order, and specialty pharmacies [S2]

Congress cites the FTC's finding that vertically integrated PBMs have both the ability and the incentive to steer business to their own affiliated pharmacies, reducing competition and increasing drug costs for patients [S2]
The findings state that PBM pressure on independent pharmacies likely contributed to the closure of more than 7,000 pharmacies between 2019 and 2024 [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not advanced, the large conglomerates that own insurers, PBMs, and pharmacies keep their current structure — including the affiliated-pharmacy steering the FTC has flagged — for now.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Joined Warren in introducing the bill, giving it Republican support from the start

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to committee and has taken no action since — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled [S4]

against.name: The largest vertically integrated health conglomerates
against.role: Owners of the three biggest PBMs and their pharmacy businesses
against.what_they_did: Companies whose business model the bill would dismantle have publicly opposed structural PBM legislation and lobbied against it

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with two Republican cosponsors (Hawley and Marshall) and one Democratic cosponsor (Fetterman), though with only four sponsors total and no floor action to date.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated health conglomerates (insurer + PBM + pharmacy)
industries.note: These companies would have one year to divest their pharmacies, ending the ability to steer prescriptions to affiliated drugstores and to shift profits into lightly regulated pharmacy units that the bill says can evade Medical Loss Ratio limits. For patients, the same steering has meant higher drug prices, so the industry's interest here runs against the public's.

PBMs lose their captive affiliated pharmacy networks and face monthly escrow penalties of 10 percent of profits for missing divestment milestones, plus lawsuits from states and private citizens. Their market power has been documented by the FTC as raising costs for patients and plans.

Removing self-preferencing by PBM-owned pharmacies would ease the contract pressure that the bill's findings link to more than 7,000 pharmacy closures between 2019 and 2024. Community pharmacies gain customers and fairer reimbursement when the middlemen no longer own their biggest competitors.

analysis.trajectory: With roughly seven months left in the 119th Congress, only four sponsors, and no committee action since referral, the bill is likely to sit in the Judiciary Committee until the session ends. Standalone structural-separation bills like this rarely reach the floor without a committee markup and leadership scheduling, so the realistic path is expiration unless the chair acts or PBM provisions are attached to a larger bill.
